title: The lost magic of the fountain pen
gist: Benjamin Rhode argues the fountain pen is one of the very few technologies where humanity has materially regressed — nibs made between the 1920s and 1950s have never been surpassed — and that its displacement by the cheaper, waterproof, disposable ballpoint is part of a wider de-skilling of handwriting that will deny future historians the tangible archival record. He frames the surviving enthusiast market (German workhorses, unreliable Italians, the finest Japanese, custom nibmeisters and Tokyo ink blenders) as an analogue enclave in a digital age, one now being further eroded by large-language models that will correspond with each other.

themes.theme: Material regression as a rare category

insights.claim: Almost all material technology improves over time, with the rare counterexamples being Roman marine concrete, the sound of a Stradivarius, and the fountain pen — where the artefacts of the past remain superior to modern reproductions.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: Identifies the narrow class of goods where scarcity is genuinely irreplaceable — the underlying logic behind durable collector-market premia.
insights.quote: Culture and politics aside, examples of material regression are less evident.
insights.locator: Mankind now makes most things better

insights.claim: The fountain pen reached its technical apex between roughly the 1920s and 1950s during an age of mass literacy and ubiquitous handwritten correspondence, and the quality and variety of nibs made then have never been surpassed.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: A fixed, non-replicable supply of peak-quality vintage nibs underpins a persistent secondary market — the classic condition for appreciating collectibles.
insights.quote: The quality and variety of nibs made then have never been surpassed.

insights.claim: The fountain pen's advantage over the quill and steel dip-pen was continuous flow without repeated replenishment, portability with its own inkwell, and near-zero writing pressure — making writing a physical as well as intellectual pleasure.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: A reminder that adoption of a tool turns on friction removal in the user's workflow, not on abstract capability.
insights.quote: It allowed words to flow as fast as one’s thoughts.
insights.locator: Unlike the quill or steel dip-pen

insights.claim: Winston Churchill in 1908 described true happiness as sitting at one's table on a sunny morning with four clear hours of uninterruptible security, plenty of nice white paper and a fountain pen.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: Evidence of how central the tool once was to elite intellectual production, which frames the scale of the cultural loss being described.
insights.quote: with four clear hours of uninterruptible security, plenty of nice white paper, and a [fountain] pen – that is true happiness.
insights.locator: ‘To sit at one’s table on a sunny morning’

insights.claim: The ballpoint displaced the fountain pen despite requiring more hand-cramping pressure and producing a sticky, uninspiring line, because its ink was waterproof, it did not leak even at altitude on aeroplanes, and it was cheap, reliable and disposable.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: A textbook case of the technically inferior but more robust and disposable product winning on total cost and reliability — the disruption pattern that repeats across categories.
insights.quote: Although it required more hand-cramping pressure and produced a rather sticky and uninspiring line on the page, the ballpoint’s ink was waterproof.
insights.locator: By the mid-century, however, the fountain pen faced competition

insights.claim: School fountain pens degraded the category's reputation for a whole generation, being charmless tools with narrow uncomfortable sections, prone to leaking, and loaded with cartridges of insipid ink in mandated uniform black or blue.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: A poor-quality mandated introduction can permanently poison consumer perception of a product category — a brand risk lesson beyond stationery.
insights.locator: The fountain pen endured, but most readers above a certain age

themes.theme: De-skilling of handwriting and the archival loss

insights.claim: Handwriting is now an increasingly archaic skill, with many people unable to write even inelegant cursive and their penmanship limited to awkwardly printing names or scrawling signatures on official forms.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: A generational skill loss that shrinks the addressable market for all handwriting-dependent products, including premium stationery.
insights.quote: Today, handwriting itself is an increasingly archaic skill
insights.locator: Many younger readers will have been denied even that

insights.claim: Rising postal delivery prices made letters both much more expensive and much more unreliable, accelerating the decline of handwritten correspondence independently of digital substitution.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: Postal cost inflation is a second, under-noticed driver of correspondence decline — a demand-side headwind for postal operators that compounds itself.
insights.quote: before the increases in the price of postal delivery made sending letters both much more expensive and much more unreliable
insights.locator: It was an effective way of signalling

insights.claim: Future historians of the present age will be denied the concrete, emotional way of knowing an ancestor that comes from deciphering a dead person's handwriting and recognising a familiar hand across different national archives.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: The digital transition is destroying a class of historical evidence, not just changing its format — a permanent narrowing of the future record.
insights.locator: Something else is lost with the disappearance

insights.claim: Almost all written composition is now digital, and it may soon become essentially de-skilled and dehumanised by the universal use of large-language models, which will effectively correspond with each other.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: The end state the author foresees is machine-to-machine correspondence with humans removed from the loop — the deepest second-order cost of LLM adoption in writing.
insights.quote: soon that, too, may become essentially de-skilled and dehumanised by the universal use of large-language models, which will effectively correspond with each other
insights.locator: Almost all written composition is now digital

insights.claim: Some research suggests memories are retained more effectively by handwriting notes than by typing them, giving the fountain pen a claimed cognitive benefit alongside aesthetic and ergonomic ones.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: The functional case for analogue note-taking is the most defensible commercial hook for premium paper and pen brands.
insights.locator: these new acolytes can preach of cognitive benefits

themes.theme: The analogue enclave and its market structure

insights.claim: Modern fountain pens are dominated by brands whose national stereotypes are manifest: German firms make solid workhorse pens, Italian models are beautiful but often unreliable, and arguably the finest are Japanese, from a country that specialises in perfecting foreign inventions and still valorises the analogue and artisanal.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: Japan's comparative advantage in perfecting imported inventions while sustaining an analogue premium culture is a durable export characteristic beyond stationery.
insights.quote: arguably the finest are Japanese, hailing from a country that specialises in perfecting foreign inventions and which still valorises the analogue, the artisanal and everything paper-based
insights.locator: In their modern incarnation, fountain pens are dominated by brands

insights.claim: A good contemporary fountain pen can be bought for less than £30, while much pricier pens are typically purchased as collector's items or corporate gifts never to be used — cost does not necessarily correlate with quality.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: The luxury pen market prices status and gifting rather than function, meaning premium brands are exposed to corporate gifting cycles rather than writing demand.
insights.quote: Cost does not necessarily correlate with quality.
insights.locator: Although they will generally not match their forebears

insights.claim: Gold nibs, being softer than steel, tend to shape themselves to their owner's handwriting, supporting a fantasy of owning something individual and personalised despite factory origin — and dedicated 'nibmeisters' can tune a nib to a customer's preference.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: Mass-produced goods that physically adapt to their owner command a personalisation premium — a product-design lever applicable well beyond pens.
insights.quote: The associated fantasy is of owning something individual and personalised, despite its being born in a factory.
insights.locator: Nibs made not of steel but of softer gold

insights.claim: The enthusiast economy runs on a growing online community cataloguing experiments across dozens of papers, hundreds of pens and thousands of ink shades, physical 'pen shows' for trading, and a viral acquisition dynamic in which 'pen addicts' become 'penablers' who recruit new converts.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: A self-propagating referral loop plus a combinatorial product space is the structural reason niche analogue hobbies keep growing revenue despite category decline.
insights.locator: For those still willing or weird enough

insights.claim: Artisanal ink-mixers in Tokyo offer custom blends based on any colour or emotional inspiration, and iron gall inks slowly cure and darken as they oxidise on the page in the manner of historical blue-black inks.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: Bespoke-to-order manufacturing at consumer price points is how a declining category sustains margin — a replicable playbook for legacy goods.
insights.locator: some of them enclosed in beautiful glass bottles

insights.claim: Attempting to match the exact blue shading ink Sigmund Freud used in a 1925 letter, artificial intelligence agreed with the author's own approximation using the Polish-made 'KWZ iron gall turquoise' while Tokyo's artisanal ink-mixers somewhat missed the mark.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: A small but telling case of AI outperforming human specialists at a perceptual matching task inside a deeply artisanal domain.
insights.locator: Online obsessives debate how to reproduce

insights.claim: It is delusional to imagine any purchasable object can confer writing talent, just as those buying pricey Leica cameras hoping to channel Henri Cartier-Bresson will be disappointed.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: The author concedes that the premium-tool market sells aspiration rather than capability — the honest basis on which luxury creative-goods demand rests.
insights.quote: It is delusional to imagine that any purchasable object could confer writing talent
insights.locator: It is delusional to imagine that any purchasable object

insights.claim: The fountain pen persists as a creative technology invested with emotions and aspirations — an analogue enclave in a digital age representing a desire to connect with the dead and living and to defy a loss that is both material and cultural.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Rhode
insights.so_what: The demand driver is meaning and continuity, not utility — which is why analogue niches survive even after their functional case collapses.
insights.quote: it also represents an analogue enclave in a digital age
insights.locator: All this may be understood as an affectation
